title: Poems Come By Chance
subtitle: I am grateful for the times I felt exhausted and uninspired, yet never put down my pen.

trails.title: To Camille
trails.description: Literature may be divided into countless intricate schools, yet what it ultimately conveys is remarkably simple.

content.text:
Dear Camille,

How long has it been since we last spoke? The long tug-of-war with the cold drained all my energy. Only today did I manage to warm up enough to dip my tail in ink and write to you.

Sylvie is doing well. Maxime and Alexandre always help her think in parallel, and Monique, as usual, keeps things under control at critical moments. Serpentes has been showing more and more signs of thought lately. I think it's only a matter of time before he speaks. Hélène is sleepier than ever, staying in heated rooms around the clock.

As for Chantal and Pierre, they're the same as always.

And me? I didn't just hibernate. The local literature has filled the gaps in my collection that Sylvie once ruthlessly discarded.

The Melusines were deeply moved by these authors' vivid portrayals of suffering and death, yet even within the darkest themes, the authors' exploration of new paths brimmed with vitality, dreams, and a defiant sense of romanticism.

Whenever I read the literature to her, her memories become unusually vivid, and she recalls one line in particular with striking clarity from Pasternak's February: "The truest verses arise by chance, tempered in the fire of pain."

Of course, there's no way to verify this and Sylvie would never admit it, but I believe she's the most romantic in our family. Or maybe the second-most. After me. I wish you were part of the Dubois family too. That way, you'll truly understand what Sylvie's memories feel like when she sees a shooting star.

I truly hope we can talk about all of this someday. Maybe after Sylvie's little challenge is complete, you could visit Plesetsk. I promise Sylvie and I will both be warmly waiting to welcome you.

Your dear friend,

Estelle

items.text: Silence has weight. Like sand piling, layer on layer, on one's chest, eventually it can suffocate.
The sobs barely register—two or three, snuffed out before they can burst.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: I will complete my mission.
She speaks with clarity, as if making a solemn vow.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: And if I successfully come back with the data, I'll consider joining Laplace.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: But I can't make a decision now. I need more time to think.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: I will stay until my job is done. You don't have to worry about that.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: That is what Mr. and Mrs. Koslov and my friends in the circus would all want. It is the right thing to do.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: If you'll excuse me, I should return to my training. I'll see you later.
She's already on the move before the last word is spoken, leaving behind another layer of suffocating silence.
It doesn't take long before someone else tries to wriggle out from it, too.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: Us too. Need to double-check the warehouse inventory. Might find something useful.

items.speaker: Han Zhang
items.text: Wait, haven't we done that already? Those—

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: Alright! We'll let you know if we find anything.
They leave the room one after another. In the corner, Voyager seems entirely unsure of what to do.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Join them if you want. I have some unfinished business.
Moments later, the last light-footed silhouette exits the room.
The familiar gold glint rests at the far end of the hallway, her head lowered against the wall.
Voyager tries to approach but hesitates, stopping mid-step.
She looks around to make sure the hallway is empty, then lifts her violin onto her shoulder.

items.speaker: Voyager
items.text: Alia!
The music strings and her voice twist together like a trembling thread, calling her friend to turn around.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Was that you? Did you just say my name?

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: You learned how to—
As she sees those flickering sparks, her voice falters.
Then, in a heartbeat, Voyager resumes her usual appearance.

items.speaker: Voyager
items.text: Stars ... good.

items.speaker: Voyager
items.text: Alia, happy.
Hissabeth has the office to herself for once, but the progress she had hoped would come to her is still elusive.
After yet another failed calculation, she sets her pen down and reconsiders her goals.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: These calculations need to be finished today.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: The "Teleport" ritual requires the caster to recite the location. It could be understood as calibrating in a way.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Let's continue with that thought.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: The destination must be preset, and the ritual cast through incantation ... But the further the distance, the harder it is to stay on target.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: If only there were an arcane reaction strong enough and unique enough to calibrate to ...
It's only then that she notices the strangeness of the moment, which is abruptly broken by the arcane energy monitor as it lets out an ear-splitting alarm.
A blinding light flashes across the entire screen, then cuts out.
The instrument's detection radius is small, barely beyond the nearby hallway.
She narrowly avoids a full-on collision in the doorway.
Luckily, she catches herself using the girl's shoulder.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: What happened? Are you alright, Ms. Hissabeth?

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Was that you? Did you cast that arcane skill just now?

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: No, those energy levels were too high for you—beyond most arcanists. Who was with you just now?

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Voyager.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: She was just trying to make me feel better. Did it interfere with your experiments? I apologize, Ms. Hissabeth. I promise it won't happen again.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: She just left. If you want to find her, I'll go with you.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Are you saying she was the one that cast that arcane skill?

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Yes. It was so pretty. It was like ...

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: A neutron star.
It's obvious that the concept is beyond Kiperina. She tilts her head expectantly.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: It's a type of highly magnetized star that emits powerful beams that can be traced to show us its precise location. We call them the beacons of space.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Such a strong arcane reaction would be so bright that it'd be trivial to locate even from an extreme distance!

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: I don't know much about space, but it sounds like the difference between finding a star in the sky and looking for the sun.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: But then the universe is also very big. I imagine if you were looking from far enough away, even the sun would seem small.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Damn! I'm afraid you're right. When comparing all the stars in the observable universe, our sun is far from the largest or brightest. Only the closest. We can't assume proximity in our case.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: But then, there's still got to be a way, non?
Capturing the fleeting aura, she propels a new train of thought forward.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Before the "Storm" arrives, the levels of arcane energy in all affected areas will be greatly amplified. But, what about places that won't be affected?

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Perhaps then, the trick will not be to look for the light in darkness, but for the darkness in the light, like finding a dim bulb in a string of Christmas lights.
Hissabeth places her hands on Kiperina's shoulders and makes a promise.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: If that's the case, I can adjust the portion of runium in order to focus the disk precisely on Plesetsk!

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: If this works out—

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Then I guarantee you will arrive home safe and sound.

1987, Plesetsk
2 months before the "Storm"

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: Understood. Take care.
She ends the call and waves at the silhouette walking her way.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: What are you up to?

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: I've been communicating with the garrison in Mirny. They've picked up some abnormal critter activity during their patrols.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: Another batch of residents is set to evacuate too. I'll head over to help them shortly.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: What about you—your geological survey? Are you staying at the branch, or will you head back to HQ?

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: Haven't found anything that's worth digging up yet, but I've decided to give it another try. Should be back here in time for the evacuation.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: Though I'm hoping to stick around for my little apprentice. She said she'll only give us her decision on joining Laplace once she's back from her mission. I can't wait to hear the good news.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: You still pretending not to care?

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: My concern, whether it exists or not, will have no tangible effect on their results. I just hope they don't kill themselves for nothing.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: Hissabeth is planning a final teleportation test the day after tomorrow. I'll be observing from the meeting room.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: You know the one we always use upstairs? Early in the afternoon.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: I'll likely be in Mirny by then.
A brief silence follows. In the pause, Windsong deftly shifts the topic to the conspicuous glass tank in the crowd.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: Hey, Ulrich! We meet again.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: You look even worse than when we last met.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Ah, Ms. Windsong? And Pointer?

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: What have we here, two of our busiest bees working together in the Plesetsk Branch?
Pointer has no idea why Ulrich looks "even worse." His expression, as ever, is nigh unreadable, so she simply nods to him.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: So, when is this "humanitarian vacation" of yours over? Any interest in sparing a little time to watch something fun?

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: If by "something fun" you mean Dmitry's party, then thanks, but no, thanks.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: No, not that. I told you about it before—Hissabeth's teleport disk experiment.

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: Ah, yes, that one. You know word of it is already spreading through HQ and all the other branches?

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: And? What's the impression?

items.speaker: Ulrich
items.text: I wouldn't categorize it as "good," but it has certainly become a contentious topic.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: At least one of the bigwigs is supportive—Madam Lucy. It seems she intends to keep our experiment going either way. She even invited a prominent String-Theory Researcher to HQ.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: As I said, even if we don't get the results we hoped for, the work itself can be illuminating.
The silent researcher at last offers a wave to attract the attention of the room.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: Excuse me. I have obligations to attend to.

items.speaker: Pointer
items.text: Let's talk again later.
She walks off, leaving Ulrich and Windsong to watch her as her figure passes into the hall and away.
Several minutes pass, then Windsong gasps.

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: S**t! I forgot my badge, and Pointer's gone. How am I supposed to get back to the lab?

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: Sorry, Ulrich, do you mind walking me back?

items.speaker: Windsong
items.text: By the way, you didn't answer whether you'll be at Hissabeth's experiment.
